cards.front: Recall a key point about School Processes & the Hidden Curriculum
cards.back: Labelling: teachers attach labels to students based on assumptions about ability, behaviour and background. Becker: teachers have an 'ideal pupil' image (middle-class, well-behaved, motivated) and judge students against it. Raynor: teachers labelled students as 'bright' or 'difficult' based on appearance and behaviour, not ability. Labels become self-fulfilling prophecies (Rosenthal & Jacobson: Pygmalion in the Classroom).

cards.front: Recall a key point about School Processes & the Hidden Curriculum
cards.back: Streaming and setting: ability grouping within schools. Streaming: broad ability groups across all subjects. Setting: ability groups within individual subjects. Ball found that working-class and ethnic minority students are over-represented in lower streams. Once placed in a lower stream, it is very difficult to move up - streams become self-perpetuating.

cards.front: Recall a key point about School Processes & the Hidden Curriculum
cards.back: Pupil subcultures: pro-school subculture (accept school values, work hard, aim for qualifications - typically in higher streams) and anti-school subculture (reject school values, disrupt lessons, seek status through deviance - typically in lower streams). Hargreaves: streaming creates anti-school subcultures because lower-stream students suffer a loss of self-esteem and seek status through alternative means.

cards.front: Recall a key point about School Processes & the Hidden Curriculum
cards.back: Lacey's concepts: differentiation (teachers label and categorise students as 'bright' or 'thick') and polarisation (students respond by moving towards pro-school or anti-school subcultures). Woods identified more responses: ingratiation (trying to please teachers), ritualism (going through the motions), retreatism (withdrawing), rebellion (active opposition), and colonisation (minimum effort to avoid trouble).

cards.front: Recall a key point about School Processes & the Hidden Curriculum
cards.back: The hidden curriculum reinforces inequality: it teaches compliance and obedience (particularly to working-class students who will fill low-status jobs), competition (which benefits those who are already advantaged), and gender/ethnic stereotypes through curriculum content and teacher expectations.

cards.front: What should you know about sociology exam tips?
cards.back: When discussing school processes, always: show the chain from labelling to achievement outcomes, name specific studies (Becker, Hargreaves, Lacey, Ball), and evaluate whether school processes create inequality or merely reflect external differences.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Streaming helps all students because they learn at their own pace with students of similar ability.
